subject: Computer Networking
title: Zero-Day Vulnerabilities
description: A quick, practical guide to Zero-Day Vulnerabilities.

hook.text: A flaw exists in software that nobody knows about — except the attacker. That's a zero-day.

buildup.text: Zero-day means zero days of warning. There's no patch available because the vendor doesn't know yet.

discovery.text: Governments and criminal groups stockpile zero-days. Some sell for millions on dark markets.

twist.text: Stuxnet used four zero-days at once to sabotage Iranian nuclear centrifuges. The most sophisticated cyberweapon ever.

climax.text: Bug bounty programs pay researchers to find and report vulnerabilities before attackers do. Prevention beats cure.

punchline.text: Zero-days are the unknown unknowns. You can't patch what you can't see.

quiz.question: What makes a zero-day vulnerability dangerous?
options: No patch exists because the vendor is unaware of it
It only affects devices manufactured on a specific day
It requires physical access to exploit

details.summary: Zero-day vulnerabilities are security flaws discovered by attackers before the software vendor knows about them, leaving zero days for the vendor to create a fix.
details.whyItMatters: Zero-days bypass all signature-based security controls. Understanding them explains why defense-in-depth, behavioral detection, and rapid patching are essential security strategies.
takeaways: Zero-days are unknown to the vendor when first exploited
No patch exists when the attack begins, making defense difficult
Behavioral detection and defense-in-depth mitigate zero-day risk

faq.question: How are zero-day vulnerabilities discovered?
faq.answer: Security researchers find them through code review, fuzzing, and reverse engineering. Some are sold on the black market. Government agencies stockpile some for intelligence purposes. Bug bounty programs incentivize responsible disclosure.

faq.question: How can you defend against zero-day attacks?
faq.answer: No single defense stops zero-days. Layer defenses: network segmentation limits spread, endpoint detection identifies anomalous behavior, application whitelisting prevents unauthorized execution, and least privilege limits damage.
